titleStmt.title: Memorial concerning the employment in the military service of the country of Prussian or German subjects who are in the service of foreign missions.

opener.seg: [Translation of the memorial accompanying the foregoing inclosure.]

head.hi: Memorial concerning the employment in the military service of the country of Prussian or German subjects who are in the service of foreign missions.

div.p: In Prussia the principle has always been maintained that Prussian subjects who are in the service of foreign ministers accredited here, or of members of foreign legations, are subject to military service in this country.

In accordance herewith all the ministers at that time accredited here were, by a circular of July 7, 1821, requested to discharge as soon as it should become necessary the Prussian subjects in their service in order that they might be enrolled in the standing army, and, in case they should belong to the reserve or “Landwehr,” to instruct them to punctually perform the military duties thereby entailed. German military legislation has made no change affecting this principle.

No objection has hitherto been raised by foreign missions here against the application of this principle; on the other hand, several foreign ambassadors and ministers have expressly recognized the justice of the position assumed by this country. In the
year 1866 two coachmen of the then French ambassador were summoned to the flag; in the year 1870–’71 servants of the then Italian minister and of the English secretary of embassy, O’Connor, as well as a garcon de chancellerie of the Belgian legation, were called to the army. In none of these cases did the chief of mission make objections. This legislation and practice which obtains in Germany and Prussia is not in conflict with international law. The latter, it is true, accords to ministers, as against the government to which they are accredited, a claim to immunity from the jurisdiction and from public burdens and taxes; a like exemption is, as a rule, conceded to the suite and servants.

As regards the materially different case, where personages of a legation are subjects of the state to which they are accredited, there is a lack in international law of positive generally recognized principles. It must therefore be left to the legislation of the individual states to fix the legal status of such persons, and in so far as no particular status has been accorded them by legislation in this country, the common law of their state will also apply to them. They are therefore subject to military duty in Germany, as German military legislation accords them no exemption.

For the correctness of this view the practice of other states also speaks. In Russia, Austria, Switzerland, and other states the privileges of exterritoriality are not conceded to subjects of the country who have entered the service of foreign missions. Nor does this appear to be the case in the United States of America. The imperial minister at Washington had in the year 1872 addressed to the government there the inquiry as to whether according to American legislation and practice American citizens in the service of foreign legations were required to pay direct municipal taxes. The Treasury Department, to whom this question was submitted for its opinion, thereupon expressed itself in a communication to the imperial minister dated May 20, 1872, as follows: “I reply to the inquiry of the German minister that the freedom from taxation by the government to which he is accredited enjoyed by a foreign minister is not understood to extend to citizens of the United States employed in the business of the legation.”
